title: Leadership, management and team culture
blurb: Show leadership from any position, build on team strengths, lead change well and influence organisations and policy.
question: A newly registered nurse says leadership is only for ward managers. A colleague points to the NMC Code. Which statement about leadership reflects the Code?

teach.body: Management is about planning, organising and controlling resources: rotas, budgets, beds, absence. Leadership is about direction and people: setting a vision, influencing, motivating and supporting others. Good nursing needs both. The Code's standard 25 asks every registrant to provide leadership to make sure people's wellbeing is protected and to improve their experiences. The NMC adds that all registrants have opportunities to show leadership, whether or not they hold a formal leadership post.

teach.h: Two sides of running a team

values: Where are we going, and why?

teach.caption: Code 25.1 blends both: identify priorities, manage time, staff and resources, and deal with risk.

head: Dimension
In practice

teach.caption: NHS Leadership Academy (2013).

teach.body: A strengths-based approach starts from what people do well and builds on it (Annexe A 4.2.1). Notice good practice, name it specifically, and give people chances to share it, teach it or lead on it. This raises motivation and spreads skills. It does not ignore problems: development needs are still agreed, but from a base of what is working.

teach.h: Leading a change on the ward

steps.label: Involve early
steps.sub: ask staff and patients for ideas

steps.label: Test small
steps.sub: a PDSA cycle on one shift

teach.caption: People support changes they have helped to shape.

teach.body: Team and organisational culture is shaped by how leaders behave: whether they thank people for reporting, admit their own mistakes and listen to concerns. Code 25.2 asks registrants to support the staff they are responsible for to follow the Code, with the knowledge, skills and competence for safe practice, and to understand how to raise concerns. Proficiency P5.12 asks nurses to understand how to influence organisational change and public policy, for example through evidence, consultations and professional bodies.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Staff Nurse Femi leads a change
teach.body: Femi, two years qualified, notices handovers on her ward overrun and miss key risks. She is not the manager, but she shares audit data at a team meeting, asks colleagues and two patients what would help, and tests a structured handover sheet for one week on nights. She asks Joy, an HCA known for her calm way with people with dementia, to add prompts about distress. After review, the team adopts the sheet and Femi shares credit with everyone involved.

teach.text: Leadership is not a job title. Code 25 applies to every registrant, and the NMC says all registrants have opportunities to show leadership regardless of formal position.

items: Management organises resources; leadership sets direction and motivates; nurses need both.
Code 25.1: identify priorities, manage time, staff and resources, deal with risk.
Code 25.2: support staff to follow the Code and to know how to raise concerns.
Build on strengths; lead change by explaining, involving, listening and testing small.
Influence policy through evidence, consultations, professional bodies and unions.

summary: You can now explain the difference between leadership and management, apply Code standard 25 whatever your role, and use the Healthcare Leadership Model and a strengths-based approach to develop a team. You can also lead change by involving people and influence organisational and public policy.

A.q: A newly registered nurse says the Code's leadership standard does not apply to her because she is not a manager. What is the most accurate reply?
options: It applies to band 7 nurses and above
All registrants can show leadership in any role
It applies once preceptorship is complete
It applies to nurses who supervise any students
A.why: Code standard 25 applies to every registrant; the NMC states that all registrants have opportunities to demonstrate leadership regardless of whether they hold formal leadership positions (P5.6).

whyNot.0: The Code does not link the leadership standard to pay band.
whyNot.2: Leadership expectations apply from registration, not after preceptorship.
whyNot.3: Supervising students is one setting for leadership, but the standard applies to all registrants.

A.q: Which of these is part of Code 25.1?
options: Refuse all but the most trivial gifts from patients
Complete records at the time or soon after an event
Keep to the laws on mental capacity where you practise
Identify priorities; manage time, staff and resources
A.why: Code 25.1: identify priorities, manage time, staff and resources effectively and deal with risk to make sure that the quality of care is maintained and improved, putting the needs of those receiving care first.

A.q: A ward sister arranges study days and stretch roles so that each nurse can grow. Which Healthcare Leadership Model dimension does this best show?
options: Developing capability
Holding to account
Evaluating information
Connecting our service
A.why: Developing capability means providing opportunities for individuals and teams to develop, building longer-term capability (NHS Leadership Academy, Healthcare Leadership Model).

whyNot.1: Holding to account is about clear expectations and challenge for improvement.
whyNot.2: Evaluating information is about using data and evidence to make decisions.
whyNot.3: Connecting our service is about understanding how parts of the system relate.

B.q: A ward is moving to electronic observations. Several experienced nurses are worried it will slow them down. What is the best way to lead the change?
options: Involve them early, explain why and pilot it
Set a firm go-live date and enforce it
Let staff who are worried keep paper charts
Ask the IT team to deliver all of the training
B.why: Effective change involves the people affected: explain why the change is needed, listen to and address concerns, and test it on a small scale so staff can shape it (P5.1; AnnexA.4.2.1; Model for Improvement).

whyNot.1: Imposing change without engagement increases resistance and misses useful concerns.
whyNot.2: Running two systems creates confusion and risk.
whyNot.3: Training matters, but leaving it to IT does not address staff concerns or ownership.

B.q: Joy, a healthcare assistant, is very skilled at calming people with dementia who are distressed. How can the nurse in charge best use a strengths-based approach?
options: Assign Joy to every patient with dementia on each shift
Invite Joy to share her approach with the team
Mention Joy's skill at her annual appraisal
Ask Joy to write the ward's dementia policy
B.why: Strengths-based team development recognises what people do well and builds on it, for example enabling a team member to share skills so others improve (AnnexA.4.2.1; P5.2).

whyNot.0: Overloading one person is not development and is unsustainable.
whyNot.2: Waiting for the appraisal misses the chance to spread good practice now.
whyNot.3: Writing policy is a different skill and responsibility from her practical strength.

B.q: Which activity is most clearly an example of leadership rather than management?
options: Completing the off-duty rota for next month
Checking the ward's monthly budget statement
Setting a shared vision and motivating the team
Recording staff sickness absence on the HR system
B.why: Setting a shared vision and motivating people are leadership behaviours in the NHS Healthcare Leadership Model (2013), under 'Sharing the vision' and 'Engaging the team'. Rotas, budgets and absence records organise resources, which is management work (P5.1).

whyNot.0: The rota is a management task of organising resources.
whyNot.1: Budget monitoring is a management task.
whyNot.3: Recording absence is a management and administrative task.

C.q: Marco, a new staff nurse from overseas, tells his team leader he does not know how to raise a concern about unsafe practice in this trust. What does Code 25.2 expect of the team leader?
options: Tell him to email the NMC directly if worried
Advise him to wait until he has settled in
Ask him to discuss concerns with colleagues first
Make sure he understands how to raise concerns
C.why: Code 25.2: support any staff you are responsible for to follow the Code, with the knowledge, skills and competence for safe practice, and to understand how to raise any concerns.

whyNot.0: The regulator is a later stage; staff should know the local routes first (NMC Raising concerns).
whyNot.1: Delaying leaves him unable to act on safety concerns now.
whyNot.2: Informal chats are not the trust's route for raising concerns.

C.q: The local integrated care board is consulting on closing a community clinic used by many of Asha's patients. How can she best influence the decision, in line with proficiency P5.12?
options: Discuss her political views with patients at clinic
Share patients' stories on social media to build support
Respond to the consultation with evidence of local need
Advise patients not to use the replacement service
C.why: P5.12 asks nurses to understand mechanisms for influencing organisational change and public policy. Responding to consultations with anonymised evidence, individually or through professional bodies and unions, is legitimate and effective (Code 20.7; Code 5).

whyNot.0: Code 20.7 says not to express personal political views inappropriately to people in your care.
whyNot.1: Posting patients' stories risks breaching confidentiality and social media guidance.
whyNot.3: Discouraging use of a service could harm patients and is not professional influence.

C.q: A new ward manager finds that staff stopped reporting errors after the previous manager criticised people at team meetings. What should she do first to change the culture?
options: Model openness, thank reporters, share learning
Make incident reporting a mandatory weekly target
Ask the previous manager to apologise to the team
Remind staff that failing to report is misconduct
C.why: Culture is shaped by leaders' behaviour. Modelling openness, thanking staff for reporting and sharing learning builds the just, open culture that reporting depends on (P5.1; Code 25.1; PSIRF).

whyNot.1: Targets without trust may produce low-quality reports and do not address fear.
whyNot.2: Seeking an apology focuses on the past rather than building new behaviour.
whyNot.3: Threats reinforce fear, the very thing stopping reporting.

reteach.title: Captain and navigator
reteach.question: On a ship, who decides where to go, and who makes sure there is enough fuel?

blocks.body: Leadership is the captain choosing a destination and getting the crew to want to go there. Management is the navigator making sure there is fuel, food and a working engine. A ward needs both, and on a ward anyone can take the captain's role for a moment: spotting a problem, proposing a better way and bringing people with them.

values: Ask why, involve team, test a fix

blocks.text: Leadership is not authority. A staff nurse who speaks up, shares good practice or leads a small change is showing leadership (Code 25).

explain.body: Provide leadership to make sure people's wellbeing is protected and to improve their experiences. 25.1: priorities, resources and risk. 25.2: support staff to follow the Code and raise concerns.

head: Clause
Requires
rows: Support staff to follow the Code and raise concerns

test.q: Which Code standard asks registrants to provide leadership to protect people's wellbeing and improve their experiences?
options: Standard 8
Standard 11
Standard 20
Standard 25
test.why: Code standard 25: provide leadership to make sure people's wellbeing is protected and to improve their experiences of the health and care system.

whyNot.1: Standard 11 is about accountability for delegation.
whyNot.2: Standard 20 is about upholding the reputation of the profession.

explain.body: Nine dimensions: inspiring shared purpose, leading with care, evaluating information, connecting our service, sharing the vision, engaging the team, holding to account, developing capability, influencing for results.

test.q: A nurse uses patient feedback and falls data to decide which improvement to prioritise. Which Healthcare Leadership Model dimension is this?
options: Leading with care
Sharing the vision
Engaging the team
Evaluating information
test.why: Evaluating information is about analysing data from different sources, such as outcomes and patient feedback, to make informed decisions (NHS Leadership Academy).

whyNot.0: Leading with care focuses on recognising and supporting the team's needs.
whyNot.1: Sharing the vision is about communicating a clear, credible direction.
whyNot.2: Engaging the team is about trusting people and inviting participation.

explain.body: Explain why, involve people early, listen and act on concerns, test the change on a small scale, then review and share results.

test.q: Staff are resistant to a new medicines round process. What is the most effective first step for the nurse leading the change?
options: Report the resistant staff to the ward manager
Listen to concerns and involve them in testing it
Introduce the new process on all shifts in the same week
Postpone the change for another year
test.why: Listening to concerns and involving staff in testing a change builds ownership and often improves the change itself (P5.1; AnnexA.4.2.1).

whyNot.0: Treating concerns as misconduct increases resistance and damages trust.
whyNot.2: A full launch without engagement or testing increases risk.
whyNot.3: Postponing without engagement does not address the concerns or the problem.

explain.body: Notice what people do well, name it specifically, give them the chance to share or teach it, and agree development from that base (AnnexA.4.2.1).

test.q: Which action best reflects a strengths-based approach to team development?
options: Listing each nurse's weaknesses at appraisal
Rotating everyone equally to avoid any favouritism
Sending the whole team on the same external course
Asking a skilled nurse to teach her technique
test.why: A strengths-based approach builds on what people do well, for example by enabling them to share skills with colleagues (AnnexA.4.2.1).

whyNot.0: Starting from weaknesses is the opposite of a strengths-based approach.
whyNot.1: Equal rotation may be fair but does not build on individual strengths.
whyNot.2: A uniform course ignores the different strengths within the team.
